paragraphs.heading: What a Lévy flight is
paragraphs.text: A Lévy flight is a random walk whose step lengths follow a stable distribution, a kind of probability distribution that is heavy-tailed. When the walk happens in more than one dimension, each step heads off in a random direction, with no direction favoured over another. Later researchers stretched the name to also cover walks that hop around a discrete grid, not only ones that move through continuous space.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: Benoît Mandelbrot coined the term, naming it after Paul Lévy, and he used it for one particular rule for choosing step sizes. He gave other names to other rules. If the step sizes follow a Cauchy distribution, he called it a Cauchy flight. If they follow a normal distribution, he called it a Rayleigh flight, and a normal distribution is not heavy-tailed.

paragraphs.heading: How it behaves over many steps
paragraphs.text: By the way they are built, Lévy flights are Markov processes. For a broad family of step-size rules that meet a power-like condition, the walker's distance from where it started settles, after very many steps, into a stable distribution. This follows from the generalized central limit theorem, and it is why so many processes can be modelled as Lévy flights. Because the step lengths scale exponentially, the pattern looks alike at every scale, so Lévy flights are used to model data that clusters.

paragraphs.heading: Where it gets used
paragraphs.text: The idea grew out of the mathematics of chaos theory. It helps with stochastic measurement and with simulating natural events that are random or pseudo-random. Uses include analysing earthquake data, financial mathematics, cryptography and signal analysis, along with many problems in astronomy, biology and physics. Even the record of ancient climates fits: the way climate jumped from one state to another there can be described as a Lévy flight.

paragraphs.heading: Predators searching the ocean
paragraphs.text: When sharks and other ocean predators fail to find food, they switch from Brownian motion, the random jiggle seen in swirling gas molecules, to a Lévy flight that mixes long runs with short, random moves. Researchers studied more than 12 million movements logged over 5,700 days by 55 tagged animals. These came from 14 predator species in the Atlantic and Pacific, among them silky sharks, yellowfin tuna, blue marlin and swordfish. Their hunting patterns could be described as Lévy flights mixed with stretches of Brownian motion.

paragraphs.heading: A hungry beetle
paragraphs.text: The paths of birds and other animals, humans included, have been modelled as Lévy flights, for example while they search for food. One beetle, Pterostichus melanarius, follows such patterns. When these beetles are hungry and food is scarce, they stay away from spots that other beetles of their kind have already searched. That habit works best for prey that is spread out widely and may not be eaten all at once, such as slugs.

paragraphs.heading: Particles and networks
paragraphs.text: Lévy walks turn up in high-energy particle physics too. Observations point to Lévy processes in collisions between heavy ions at high energy. In a network, efficient routing can be done with links whose lengths follow a Lévy flight distribution with particular values of alpha.
